title: Ecological succession

definition.text: The way the mix of species in an ecological community changes over time.

facts.text: There are two main kinds: primary succession, on newly created ground with no life, and secondary succession, after a disturbance such as fire destroys an existing community.
Succession is driven by feedbacks: growing plants create shade, add organic matter to soil and change nutrient supply, opening room for different plants.
Early-succession communities are dominated by fast-growing, well-dispersed species.
As a community approaches climax, species diversity, plant biomass and stability rise, while net primary productivity and nutrient cycling rates fall.
A tilled-up grassland is estimated to need at least 100 years, and potentially 1,400 years on average, to regain its earlier biodiversity.
Succession is shaped both by whether seeds can reach a site (dispersal limitation) and whether they can survive there (environmental filtering).
How much random chance, versus deterministic factors, steers succession is debated.

contested_note: Ecologists debate how far random events, rather than deterministic factors, set the path of succession.

definition.text: Succession that begins when life first colonizes an area with little or no living matter.

facts.text: It starts on surfaces such as newly exposed rock or sand, lava flows and freshly exposed glacial till.
Its stages run from pioneer species such as microorganisms, lichens and mosses, through grasses and small shrubs, to trees.

definition.text: In classical theory, the end point of succession, where the community is in steady balance with its environment and persists unless heavily disturbed.

facts.text: A climax community is described as having wide species diversity and complex food chains.
At climax, gross primary production is balanced by total respiration, and nutrient uptake from soil is balanced by nutrient return in litter fall.
Frederic Clements held that succession converges on a climate-determined stable climax; modern ecologists have largely abandoned this idea for nonequilibrium views.
Intermediate stages on the way to climax are called seral communities.

definition.text: A transition zone where two plant communities meet and blend.

facts.text: Examples include estuaries, lagoons, salt marshes, riparian zones and the zone between grassland and forest.
An ecotone can be narrow or wide, local or regional, and may show as a gradual blending or a sharp boundary.
Ecotones matter for mobile animals, which can use more than one set of habitats within a short distance.
The greater variety of plants and animals where communities meet is called the edge effect.

definition.text: A physical transition zone between two systems, where the environment changes along one or two physical or chemical factors.

facts.text: An ecocline can be a gradient in temperature (thermocline), chemistry (chemocline), salinity (halocline) or water density (pycnocline).
Ecoclines are less clear-cut and more stable than ecotones, so they hold higher plant species richness.
